newsitem.title: USA: Dole "listens to America," but what is it saying?.
newsitem.headline: Dole "listens to America," but what is it saying?.

text.p: Bob Dole calls it "listening to America."
Hopscotching his way across the Midwest this week, the Republican presidential nominee has held a series of long, ostensibly unscripted question-and-answer sessions with concerned citizens.
Another way to describe the meetings would be highly orchestrated chats with faithful Republicans who come not so much to question Dole, as to praise him.

The intended audience appears to be the local television stations that turn out in droves to cover the candidate as he passes through, rather than the national media travelling with him that is interested only in hard news.
Of this, there is precious little to be had.
In the grassy courtyard of a technology company outside Detroit on Wednesday, Dole gave a tight version of his stump speech and then took a string of questions from a mostly well-dressed audience.
The first, asked by a woman in a fuschia hat and matching blouse sitting in the front row, was as follows:

"I was very fortunate last June to be a delegate to the White House conference on small business. We asked President Clinton for all the things that you have just said. He's given none of it to small business. You said you are going to do it. Wonderful. Thank you."

On Tuesday, in Colorado Springs, Colorado, a woman stood up to tell Dole he deserved to be president because he had been faithful to his wife, Elizabeth Dole, while another chimed in that "having a tastefully dressed first lady would certainly help the fashion industry."
The Dole campaign, which held its first such session in California last week, appears to be using the forums as a way to generate positive coverage from local newspapers and television stations.
While the meetings are ostensibly open to the public, access seems to be carefully controlled, with the hosts -- usually friendly local companies -- doling out most of the invitations.
"I don't know who gets into these darn things," Dole campaign spokesman Nelson Warfield told reporters after a "Listening to America" session in Des Moines, Iowa, on Wednesday morning.
"There are no quotas as to who can come," he said. "This isn't a Democratic convention."
Warfield said his understanding was that the company hosting the event, as well as the local Republican party, had sent out invitations, although some people had come without them.
The Dole campaign appears to be carefully structuring the meetings to meet the needs of local television.

At Tuesday's session in Colorado Springs, one person after another droned on from prepared statements before Dole got up to speak, precisely at 5 p.m., when the local television news broadcasts begin.
No less than six satellite and microwave trucks were set up outside to beam his words back to their stations.
